text: Most of the day, this screen is off. Turn it on, and it sells you something, or hands you a feed with no end.
Today makes it something else. It stays on, in the room she already lives in, and it holds the shape of her day. Built for the glance — coming in the door, cooking, on the way out.
It opens by bringing up the thing she's been letting slide. Her own dentist. Not to chase her — to say it hasn't forgotten.
Then she tells it about her day, however it comes out. One line. Nobody has time for a form.
She never touches the television. Five seconds later it catches up on its own, already knowing the baby was up in the night.
Remembering is the easy half. The hard half is the things that never move, because every time she thinks of one, she has to work out where to start again.
So it doesn't hand the whole thing back. It puts one move on today.
Underneath it's broken down, and every step carries the moment it fits into. But she only ever gets one. Tomorrow's arrives on its own.
Ask it something it doesn't know and it looks it up. But it doesn't hand back a search page. It reads what it found against this family.
An eight-month-old who isn't walking yet. And one line that isn't about the baby at all — which of the three is the most restful for her.
It writes what it found into the thing itself — where, what it suits, what it costs.
No shopping. No feed. No progress bars.
It won't choose for her. It tells her what each one costs her, and hands the choice back. It isn't a today. It's her today.
Today. A small tiger who keeps today for you.
